id: On the Existence of the Soul

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

How confident I am it is there. Don’t I bring it, As if it were enclosed in a fine leather case, To particular places solely for its own sake? Haven’t I set it down before the variegated canyon And the undeviating bald salt dome? Don’t I feed it on ivory calcium and ruffled Shell bellies, shore boulders, on the sight Of the petrel motionless over the sea, its splayed Feet hanging? Don’t I make sure it apprehends The invisibly fine spray more than once? I have seen that it takes in every detail I can manage concerning the garden wall and its borders. I have listed for it the comings and goings Of one hundred species of insects explicitly described. I have named the chartreuse stripe And the fimbriated antenna, the bulbed thorax And the multiple eye. I have sketched The brilliant wings of the trumpet vine and invented New vocabularies describing the interchanges between rocks And their crevices, between the holly lip And its concept of itself. And if not for its sake, why would I go Out into the night alone and stare deliberately Straight up into 15 billion years ago and more? I have cherished it. I have named it. By my own solicitations I have proof of its presence.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: How, Don, Haven

outputs.L1:
I am certain it is there. Do I not carry it, as though enclosed in a fine leather case, to particular places solely for its own sake? Have I not set it down before the variegated canyon and the unwavering bald salt dome? Do I not nourish it with ivory calcium and ruffled shell bellies, with shore boulders, and with the sight of the petrel suspended motionless above the sea, its splayed feet hanging? Do I not ensure that it apprehends the invisibly fine spray more than once?

I have seen that it absorbs every detail I can provide concerning the garden wall and its borders. I have catalogued for it the comings and goings of one hundred species of insects, each explicitly described. I have named the chartreuse stripe and the fimbriated antenna, the bulbed thorax and the multiple eye. I have sketched the brilliant wings of the trumpet vine and invented new vocabularies to describe the interchanges between rocks and their crevices, between the holly lip and its concept of itself.

And if not for its sake, why would I go out alone into the night and stare deliberately straight up into fifteen billion years ago and beyond? I have cherished it. I have named it. Through my own solicitations, I have proof of its presence.
outputs.L2:
I am certain it exists.  
After all, don’t I carry it with me,  
almost as though it rested inside an elegant leather container,  
and take it to certain places simply because it deserves to be there?  

Haven’t I placed it in front of the many-colored canyon  
and the stark, unwavering white salt dome?  
Don’t I nourish it with pale calcium, with curled shell interiors,  
with stones along the shore, with the image  
of a petrel suspended still above the ocean,  
its spread feet dangling beneath it?  

Don’t I see to it that it notices  
the almost invisible mist of spray again and again?  
I have watched it absorb every particular  
I am able to gather about the garden wall and its edges.  
For it, I have recorded the movements in and out  
of a hundred insect species, each one carefully identified.  

I have pointed out the yellow-green band,  
the fringed feeler, the rounded thorax,  
and the many-faceted eye.  
I have drawn the vivid blossoms of the trumpet vine  
and created fresh terms for the exchanges  
between stones and the cracks within them,  
between the holly’s edge  
and its own idea of what it is.  

And if I did not do all this for its benefit,  
why would I step outside by myself at night  
and intentionally look straight upward  
into a past fifteen billion years old, and beyond?  

I have cared for it tenderly.  
I have given it a name.  
Through my own acts of attention and invitation,  
I have evidence that it is truly there.
outputs.L3:
The speaker expresses a quiet but unwavering confidence in the existence of an unnamed inner presence, referred to only as “it.” This presence is not explained directly, yet it is treated as something real, valuable, and intimate. The speaker carries it carefully within themselves and brings it to places that feel meaningful, as though these settings can nourish or awaken it. Their confidence does not depend on outside confirmation; instead, it comes from the depth of their own experience and devotion.

Much of the speaker’s care for this inner presence takes the form of attention to the natural world. They expose it to rich landscapes, vivid details, and sensory experiences, as if offering it beauty, texture, and wonder. Nature becomes a kind of gift or sustenance. The speaker notices the shapes, colors, movements, and sounds around them, allowing the presence to encounter the world through these carefully chosen experiences.

This devotion is especially clear in the speaker’s habit of observing and naming natural forms. Insects, plants, rocks, and other small features of the landscape are not passed over casually. Instead, the speaker studies them closely and identifies them, suggesting that naming is an act of care. To name something is to recognize it fully, to grant it significance, and to share that significance with the hidden presence they carry. Their attention transforms ordinary details into offerings.

The speaker’s solitary contemplation of the night sky deepens this sense of devotion. Looking up at the ancient stars, they place themselves in relation to something vast, old, and mysterious. This private act of wonder becomes another way of honoring the inner “it.” The silence and solitude of the moment suggest reverence, as though the speaker is not merely observing the universe but presenting its grandeur to the presence within.

Ultimately, the speaker believes that these acts of attention, naming, and cherishing are themselves proof that the presence exists. The care they give to it, the way they shape their experiences around it, and the intensity with which they notice the world all serve as evidence. For the speaker, the existence of this inner presence is confirmed not through logical argument, but through devotion: because they carry it, nurture it, and offer the world to it, it must be real.
outputs.L4:
The speaker meditates on the presence of an inner “it,” an unnamed force that seems to live within the self. This “it” may be understood as consciousness, imagination, the soul, or some private center of being that cannot be easily defined. Rather than explaining it directly, the speaker tests its existence by carrying it through the world and observing what happens. The speaker takes it into landscapes, through natural scenes, and across remembered places, as if the only way to know whether this inner presence is real is to let it encounter the textures of life.

Throughout this process, the speaker pays close attention to details. The act of naming becomes important: by noticing trees, fields, light, water, weather, and other features of the natural world, the speaker gives shape to experience. These details do not simply describe the outer world; they also reveal the inner one. As the speaker moves through nature, memory, and time, the mysterious “it” responds. It becomes more vivid through contact with the world, as though perception awakens it.

The speaker also exposes this inner presence to larger forces: the cycles of nature, the depth of memory, and the vastness of cosmic time. In doing so, the poem or passage suggests that the self is not isolated. The inner life is connected to everything around it, from small earthly details to immense universal patterns. By placing the fragile, invisible “it” against such vastness, the speaker both tests and protects it. The act of attention becomes an act of care.

Ultimately, the speaker finds proof that this hidden presence exists. The proof does not come from logic or scientific evidence, but from devotion, perception, and sustained awareness. By carrying, naming, watching, and loving this inner “it,” the speaker makes it real. The unseen self becomes meaningful because it is attended to. In this way, the text suggests that consciousness or soul is not something separate from experience; it is discovered and strengthened through the very act of perceiving the world with care.
outputs.L5:
**How Don Found Haven**

Don had always wondered how people knew when they had found a place where they truly belonged. He had traveled through busy cities, quiet villages, and long roads that seemed to disappear into the horizon, but nowhere felt like home.

One evening, after a long day of walking, Don reached a small town called Haven. The streets were calm, the windows glowed warmly, and the people greeted him as if they had been expecting him. For the first time in years, Don felt his worries begin to fade.

He sat by a small fountain in the center of town and asked himself, “How can a place feel so familiar when I have never been here before?”

An old woman nearby smiled and said, “Haven is not just a place. It is a feeling. You find it when you stop running and allow yourself to rest.”

Don looked around and understood. Haven was not only the town’s name; it was the peace he had been searching for. From that day on, Don no longer asked how he would find his home. He knew he had already found it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem in the style of Jorie Graham about proving the existence of the soul through acts of close observation in nature.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in the exact style of Jorie Graham, but here’s an original contemporary free-verse poem that uses philosophical inquiry, close natural observation, and expansive, meditative movement.

---

**Proof by Looking**

I thought the soul would announce itself  
as radiance, as some gold-edged aperture  
opening in the chest—

but morning was busy with smaller things.

A spider, for instance, rebuilding the theorem  
of her web between two stalks of dead grass,  
each thread taking the light  
then losing it, taking it again,

as if proof were not possession  
but return.

The creek kept making its argument  
over stones: no sentence,  
only revision, revision, revision—  
water altering itself around whatever resisted.

I knelt there long enough  
for my knees to darken with earth,  
for one ant to climb the back of my hand  
and pause at the blue vein  
as if listening beneath the skin.

What did it hear?

Not music. Not meaning.  
Only the stubborn engine of being here,  
the blood’s dim weather moving  
without instruction.

A leaf detached above me  
and did not fall straight down.  
It swerved, lifted, seemed for one instant  
to reconsider gravity,

and in that hesitation  
I believed—not in escape,  
but in the hidden surplus  
inside obedience.

The fern unfurled by fractions.  
The mushroom shouldered up  
through last year’s rot.  
A fox track filled slowly with rain.

Everywhere, the world was not explaining itself.  
It was attending.

The soul, if it exists,  
must be like this:  
not a jewel sealed in the body,  
not a flame cupped against wind,

but the body’s capacity  
to be entered by what it sees—

the heron’s stillness  
becoming a room inside the watcher,  
the bee’s gold labor  
thickening the air between breaths,

the distant thunder teaching the field  
how to wait.

I cannot prove it except by noticing  
how the minnows scatter  
when my shadow crosses them,

then gather again,

each small life resuming  
its silver question.

And something in me,  
which I did not make,  
answers by widening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a meditative poem that begins with “How confident I am it is there” and treats an unnamed inner presence as something carried to landscapes, fed with sensory details, and confirmed by attention.
counterfactuals.output:
How confident I am it is there,  
though it has no face I can summon,  
no name that does not lessen it.  

I carry it into the hills  
as one carries water in a cupped hand,  
careful, yet always losing some  
to light, to motion, to the green  
breath of grass after rain.  

At the shore I feed it salt air,  
the drag and silver collapse of waves,  
gulls writing their hunger  
over the blank page of morning.  
It grows quiet, not larger,  
as if quiet were its true size.  

In the pine woods I offer resin,  
moss-dark stones, the small brown labor  
of ants beneath a fallen branch.  
I offer the sudden deer,  
then the emptiness after the deer.  

What else can I give  
but the world as it arrives—  
warm bread, woodsmoke, a blue cup,  
the bell that trembles after ringing,  
the late sun resting its hand  
on the shoulder of a wall?  

When I attend, it answers  
without speaking.  
Not by appearing,  
but by making appearance enough:  
each leaf edged in its own fire,  
each silence holding itself open,  
each breath returning  
with evidence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical philosophical poem about consciousness, using images of canyons, salt domes, insects, shells, seabirds, garden walls, and deep time.
counterfactuals.output:
In the canyon’s throat, where shadow learns to sing,  
a thought descends like water over stone,  
wearing the earth by whispering its name  
through terraces of vanished rain.

Beneath us, salt domes rise in silent prayer,  
white mountains buried under the weight of time,  
remembering seas that had no witness  
but the moon, and the moon’s cold hunger.

An insect climbs the garden wall—  
six careful legs upon the empire of brick—  
and pauses, as if the world were a question  
it could answer only by continuing.

What is consciousness, if not this pause,  
this bright hesitation between dust and wing,  
the canyon echo hearing itself return,  
the shell holding an ocean after the ocean is gone?

Seabirds carve their cries above the tide,  
brief scriptures written on the moving air.  
They do not ask who listens.  
They vanish into listening.

And deep time opens under every step:  
layer on layer of sleep and salt and bone,  
the ancient shell, the fossil leaf,  
the small black insect sealed in amber’s gold.

Still, behind the garden wall, the mind  
leans outward, flowering toward what it cannot be.  
It names the stars, then feels them naming back,  
a coastline trembling inside the skull.

Perhaps we are not lamps, but doorways—  
not the flame, but the canyon shaped by flame;  
not the sea, but the shell’s curved memory;  
not eternity, but its sudden bird

lifting from the stone,  
crying once,  
and entering the blue  
as though the blue were waking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long, single-stanza poem in which the speaker insists that “it” exists because they have shown it the natural world in painstaking detail.
counterfactuals.output: I tell you it exists because I have taken it by the hand, or what would be a hand if it had learned the grammar of bones, and led it out beyond the last porch-light, beyond the road’s pale seam, into the wet margin where the ditch keeps its cold black water and the cattails hold up their brown, patient candles; I have shown it how morning gathers first as a blue refusal in the east, then loosens, thread by thread, into gold along the backs of clouds, how dew stipples each blade of grass with a separate trembling world, how the spider’s web, invisible a moment before, becomes a harp of water and silk, every strand strung with light, every bead an eye; I have crouched beside it under the milkweed and opened the green pods with my thumb so it could see the packed, impossible softness inside, the seeds laid there like sleeping fish, each with its white plume folded close, waiting for wind to grant it a future; I have shown it the ant’s dark punctuation across the stone, the worm’s blind signature in the loosened soil, the beetle’s lacquered back shining as if night itself had condensed and learned to move; I have made it listen to the creek speaking in many mouths at once, over root, under fern, against the slick ribs of rock, carrying leaves the color of old copper, carrying pollen, shadow, the drowned reflection of a passing hawk, and I have said, hear that, how nothing repeats and yet the whole song knows itself; I have shown it the moss on the north side of the maple, not merely green but a kingdom of greens, velvet, bottle, emerald, bruised olive, the green of something kept secret and breathing under snow; I have pressed its faceless attention near the bark where the lichen blooms in maps of ash and sulfur, where the tree’s rough skin cracks into valleys and ridges, and beneath that hidden labor the sap climbs without applause, without hurry, carrying summer upward in its transparent ladders; I have shown it the foxglove’s spotted throat and the bee vanishing into it like a thought entering the body, the bee returning with its legs dusted yellow, drunk on the errand that keeps the field alive; I have shown it swallows cutting the air with black scissors, their wings writing and erasing cursive over the pond, and the pond answering with rings wherever a fish lifts its mouth to take the stunned gnat from the skin of the water; I have shown it the turtle on the half-sunk log, the ancient dome of its shell warm with sun, the red commas near its eyes, the slow withdrawal of its head as our shadows leaned too near; I have held it still for the heron’s gray patience, one foot lifted, spear of a beak aimed at the minute shiver below, then the sudden stab, the silver writhing, the throat’s solemn swallow; I have shown it rain before rain arrives, the way the leaves turn their paler undersides upward, the way the air thickens and tastes of metal, the way cattle gather under the ash and the swifts fly lower, stitching warning through the yard; I have shown it rain arriving, first one round drop darkening the dust, then another, then thousands, until the roof drums, the gutters overflow, the earth exhales that deep mineral breath no perfumer can counterfeit, and every root, hidden and essential, drinks its portion of thunder; I have shown it how the storm walks away with blue fire still flickering in its hem, and how the world, rinsed and astonished, raises the smell of crushed fern, split cedar, opened clay; I have shown it the snail’s silver road over the stone step, the small tent of the shell borne forward with a monarch’s unhurried certainty; I have shown it mushrooms lifted overnight from the dark treaty between rot and rain, ivory bells, russet shelves, orange cups holding the last coolness of dawn, and I have explained, though it did not ask, how death feeds the delicate architecture of return; I have shown it the fallen deer in the brush, not to frighten it, but to tell the whole truth: the flank already entering grass, the rib bones pearled by weather, flies with their green, jeweled urgency, the fox tracks crossing nearby, the earth accepting what the body could no longer keep; I have shown it, too, the fawn still freckled with the forest’s broken light, knees like questions, ears wide as leaves, stepping through the tall rye while its mother lifted her black nose to read our breath; I have shown it winter before the snow, the fields rubbed flat, the hedgerows full of thorn, the milkweed pods split open, the pond skinned over with the first thin pane of ice; I have shown it winter after the snow, the world reduced and magnified, each fencepost wearing a white cap, each twig outlined in silence, the rabbit’s paired prints making a scripture across the yard, the crow’s feet starring the drifts under the black walnut, the vole tunnels drawn just beneath the crust like secret roads on a map of sleep; I have shown it the river sealed at the edges but moving dark in the middle, refusing stillness, carrying under the ice the memory of mountains, springs, rain, the dissolved wings of leaves; I have shown it the breath of horses rising in white plumes at the fence, their lashes rimed, their great heads lowering to nose aside the snow and find the stubborn grass beneath; I have shown it the night sky in January, pitiless and generous, Orion lifting his bright belt over the barn, Sirius flashing like a nail driven into the cold, the Pleiades huddled blue and far, and I have said, look, even distance has texture, even absence shines if the dark is clear enough; I have shown it the moon laying a blade of light along the frozen lane, making every stone cast a blue shadow, making the owl appear only when it moved, one pale thought leaving the pine; I have shown it the owl’s pellet split apart on the windowsill, tiny skulls, threadlike bones, the record of hunger arranged without malice; I have shown it spring not as a word but as a bruise of purple crocus through snowmelt, as skunk cabbage steaming in the thawed swamp, as the redbud’s first haze along the road, as maple flowers no larger than sparks, as the peepers beginning at dusk in the marsh until the whole dark water trembles with invisible throats; I have shown it the salamander under the lifted stone, black and yellow as if night had been painted with warnings, its small feet splayed in the mud, its body cool, secret, perfect; I have shown it the nest in the gutter, twigs, hair, straw, a shred of blue plastic woven into the old design, and later the eggs, speckled and warm beneath the mother’s breast, and later still the naked chicks, blind, clamoring, all mouth and pulse, demanding the world turn into worms; I have shown it the apple tree swelling from bud to blossom, each flower pink-veined, briefly fragrant, scandalously mortal, and then the green fists of fruit forming where petals fell, the bees gone on to other errands, the branch heavier by imperceptible degrees; I have shown it summer’s abundance until there could be no denial: the corn’s green blades rasping against one another, the tomatoes splitting their red skins in the heat, the basil bruising sweet beneath the thumb, the blackberries hanging in thorny constellations, some hard and red, some soft as a held secret, some already taken by birds whose purple droppings mark the fence; I have shown it heat visible above the road, dragonflies patrolling the ditch like shards of stained glass, cicadas sawing their one note into the noon until the air itself seemed made of sound; I have shown it the copperhead’s pattern among the dead leaves, a danger shaped exactly like its hiding place, and the garter snake slipping through clover, harmless and quick as a green-black ribbon pulled by the earth; I have shown it the mare’s-tail clouds high and white before a front, the low anvils of August storms, the red sun dimmed by distant fire, the west wind carrying the smoke of forests we have never touched and yet have harmed; I have shown it the field after mowing, the sweet violence of cut stems, the kestrel hovering over what the blades exposed, the mice running their panicked errands through the fallen grass; I have shown it the garden at dusk when the squash blossoms close their golden throats, when the toad comes out from under the watering can, when moths open and shut their powdery wings against the porch screen, wanting the lamp, mistaking our small imitation for the moon; I have shown it autumn’s slow burning, sumac first, then maple, then the oak’s withheld bronze, the hickory yellow as butter, the dogwood dark red as a hidden organ, every leaf a page the tree must surrender to survive; I have shown it acorns knocking on the roof in the night, walnuts blackening in the lane, geese shouldering south in their ragged V, calling down the old instructions to one another; I have shown it the monarchs gathering in the fir before the long departure, wings closing and opening like fragments of sunset that remember Mexico; I have shown it the goldenrod bending under bees, the aster’s purple stars, the seedheads of coneflowers bristling with finches, the air full of fluff and burr and wing and the soft debris of completion; I have shown it mud, not as filth but as archive: deer cleft, raccoon hand, dog pad, boot heel, raindrop, the drag of a branch, the whole day impressed and darkening; I have shown it stone, too, granite freckled with mica, limestone holding the pale ghosts of shells from a sea lifted into hill, slate splitting in clean pages that predate our names; I have shown it the mountain from far off, blue with distance, then nearer, where spruce roots clutch the thin soil and cold springs rise clear over pebbles, each bubble carrying a shard of sky; I have shown it the sea when finally we reached it, not symbol, not vastness merely, but wrack line, kelp bulb, mussel beard, crab track, salt crust on the rail, gull cry, foam lace, the tide’s repeated argument with stone, the sandpiper’s clockwork feet chasing the withdrawal of each wave; I have shown it tide pools where anemones close at the shadow of a finger, where periwinkles seal themselves in spirals, where starfish cling with hundreds of small convictions to the underside of rock; I have shown it the horizon erasing and remaking itself all afternoon, the gray whale’s back lifting once beyond the breakers like a wet hill traveling, the spout rising and dissolving, proof that breath may appear briefly and still belong to an enormous body hidden from us; I have shown it deserts, too, because the world is not only green mercy: the creosote after rare rain, bitter and clean; the lizard’s quick stitch over sand; the cactus blooming absurdly pink from a body armed against thirst; the long shadows of evening unrolling from stones still warm enough to hold the day’s fire; I have shown it dunes that move grain by grain, mesas layered in rust and ocher, ravens balancing on thermals with nothing beneath them but space and the old patience of rock; I have shown it caves where water writes limestone into columns, drop by drop, beyond any witness, where blind fish ghost the underground pools, where the dark is so complete that even thought must feel its way forward; I have shown it forests so dense with rain that leaves grow upon leaves, bromeliads cupping water in the high branches, orchids fastening their bright mouths to bark, frogs the size of thumbnails singing from the green gloom, decay and birth crowding one another so closely no border can be drawn; I have shown it tundra, low and wind-combed, lichens like crushed moons, dwarf willow hugging the ground, caribou trails braided through the thaw, the sky immense enough to make the human heart feel like a match flame; I have shown it fireflies in the meadow rising after the longest day, their brief lamps blinking in codes older than our grief, and I have said, there, there, do you see how the dark is not empty but answered; I have shown it everything I could bear to notice, and more than I could bear: the broken wing, the late frost, the nest blown down, the poisoned stream, the plastic in the gull’s gut, the white coral bone of reefs, the orchard loud with blossoms one week and silent the next; I have shown it beauty not washed clean of terror, terror not stripped of beauty, the hawk’s shadow crossing the lamb, the parasite’s shining egg, the flood’s brown muscle lifting cars and cradles alike, the seed floating afterward in a ditch, already swollen with intention; I have shown it how the world does not argue for itself and yet persists, how roots pry sidewalks apart without philosophy, how fungus threads the forest into conversation without a tongue, how the sun spends itself on nettle and rose with the same gold hand; and if it still pretends to be nowhere, if it still hides behind the locked door of an unnamed doubt, I will bring it again to the hinge of morning and point out the frost feathers on the window, the chickadee’s black cap, the birch bark curling like paper saved from a fire, the little eddies of dust where moth wings have been, the smell of rain in a stone before the sky has darkened, the blue vein inside a leaf, the pulse under the frog’s translucent throat, the minuscule teeth along the edge of a grass blade, the pollen on my sleeve, the burr caught in my sock, the salt drying on my wrist, the ache in my knees from kneeling to see; I will say I know it exists because I have not left it in abstraction, I have not allowed it to drift unbodied through the rooms of speech, I have dragged it through bramble and bog, through orchard and marsh, through tide and snow, through the hot animal breath of barns, through the mineral hush of caves, through the pine-needle floor where mushrooms lift their soft umbrellas, through the field where every cricket scrapes the dark into being; I have given it the names of flowers and the names of weeds, though the bees make no distinction; I have given it weather, fang, feather, spoor, shell, blossom, thorn, thunderhead, watershed, moonrise, molt, migration, spawning, germination, rot; I have shown it the natural world in such painstaking detail that it has taken on weight from every stone I made it touch, color from every finch and foxglove, sound from every creek and wingbeat, scent from every crushed herb and rain-awakened field, breath from every mare in winter and whale beyond the surf; and therefore it exists, it must exist, not because I invented it, but because the world, in entering it grain by grain, has left no room inside it for nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an introspective nature poem with scientific and ornate vocabulary, centered on the idea that perception itself is evidence of an invisible beloved or soul.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Optics of the Unseen**

In the vesperal laboratory of leaves,  
where chlorophyll distills the sun to green  
and dew beads tremble like small planets  
on the cilia of the grass,  
I stand—an instrument of astonishment,  
my iris widening toward the world  
as if the world were whispering through light.

What is this seeing,  
this neural phosphorescence,  
this quiet electrophany of nerve and star,  
but testimony of a hidden hand?  
The photon dies against the retina,  
yet rises inward as form—  
elm, heron, cloud, your absent face—  
a resurrection so precise  
it feels like love disguised as physics.

Beneath the bark, capillaries of sap ascend;  
beneath my ribs, a darker xylem stirs.  
The wind combs the meadow  
with invisible fingers,  
and every blade inclines  
toward a name it cannot pronounce.  
So too my thoughts, filamented and fragrant,  
turn in their heliotropism  
toward one I cannot prove except by longing.

O unseen beloved,  
soul behind the scrim of phenomena,  
you are not an object in the field  
but the field’s luminous condition—  
the aperture through which being appears,  
the secret grammar in the cry of jays,  
the aureate theorem of moss  
proving softness against stone.

If I perceive the river’s silver calculus,  
the lichens’ patient cartography,  
the moon’s cold osculation  
upon the shoulders of the hills,  
then something in me is already met—  
some veiled cognate of the infinite  
answering from within the act of sight.

For perception is not a window only,  
but a covenant:  
the visible entering the mind  
and finding there a chamber prepared,  
a lamp already burning,  
a silence shaped exactly like reply.
